details:
**Bronze David**
Donatello's most famous work and the first freestanding male nude sculpture since antiquity, probably made for the Medici. The effeminate, boyish David stands in contrapposto with his left hand on his hip, wearing only a laurel- or flower-trimmed hat and boots, leaning on Goliath's sword with his foot on the giant's severed head. A wing from Goliath's helmet creeps up David's leg.

**Gattamelata**
Donatello's bronze equestrian statue of the Venetian mercenary (condottiero) Erasmo da Narni, nicknamed Gattamelata ("Honeyed Cat"), in the Piazza del Santo outside the Basilica of St. Anthony in Padua. Inspired by the ancient statue of Marcus Aurelius, it is the earliest surviving Renaissance equestrian bronze; the horse rests a hoof on a small orb, and the pedestal has two fake doors suggesting the gates of the underworld.

**Zuccone (Habakkuk)**
Donatello's marble statue of the prophet Habakkuk for the bell tower (Campanile) of Florence Cathedral, nicknamed "Zuccone" ("pumpkin head") because of its bald head. According to Vasari, Donatello considered it his favorite work and shouted "Speak, damn you, speak!" at it because it looked so lifelike. He also made other prophets for the Campanile, such as the "Bearded" and "Beardless" prophets.

**Penitent Magdalene**
A painted poplar-wood statue made for the Florence Baptistery, showing Mary Magdalene in her old age as a gaunt, wrinkled hermit clothed in ragged hair, with her hands pressed together in prayer. Its extreme realism may draw on icons of the emaciated hermit Mary of Egypt, and Vasari praised it highly.

**Stiacciato (schiacciato)**
An extremely shallow relief technique pioneered by Donatello, in which tiny variations in depth create the illusion of deep space, much like a drawing in stone. Its earliest surviving example is the relief St. George Freeing the Princess (St. George and the Dragon) below his St. George statue.

**St. Mark (Orsanmichele)**
Donatello's marble statue made for the linen weavers' guild's niche at Orsanmichele, the Florentine guild church. It stands in classical contrapposto, and its proportions were deliberately distorted to look correct when viewed from below in the raised niche; legend says the guild first objected to its appearance at street level.

**St. George (Orsanmichele)**
Donatello's marble statue of the warrior saint for the armorers' guild niche at Orsanmichele, now in the Bargello museum. Its base holds the stiacciato relief of St. George slaying the dragon and freeing the princess.

**Feast of Herod**
A gilded bronze relief Donatello made for the baptismal font of the Siena Cathedral Baptistery. It shows Salome's dance and the presentation of John the Baptist's head, using linear perspective and shallow relief to create deep architectural space.

**Judith and Holofernes**
Donatello's late bronze statue of the biblical heroine Judith raising a sword to behead the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes. It was cast in several separate pieces and designed to be viewed from multiple angles, and Michelangelo's David later replaced it at the Palazzo Vecchio.

**Amor-Atys**
A small bronze in the Bargello of a laughing, winged child with a faun's tail, raising his arms in the air and wearing open leggings that expose his buttocks and genitals. Its identity is unclear, combining traits of Cupid, Atys, and Mercury, such as winged sandals.

**Tomb of Antipope John XXIII**
A wall tomb in the Florence Baptistery for Baldassare Cossa, the deposed Antipope John XXIII, designed by Donatello together with his partner Michelozzo. It includes the Cossa coat of arms and allegorical figures of three Virtues.

**St. John the Evangelist**
A seated marble statue made for the facade of Florence Cathedral. Its lower body is elongated so that the figure appears correctly proportioned when seen from below, which some viewers read as a proto-Mannerist distortion.

**Chellini Madonna (Virgin and Child with Four Angels)**
A small bronze roundel that Donatello gave to his doctor, Giovanni Chellini. Its back is hollowed out as a mold so that copies could be made by pouring in molten glass.

**Bust of Niccolò da Uzzano**
A realistic painted terracotta portrait bust of the Florentine statesman Niccolò da Uzzano, attributed to Donatello and one of the earliest Renaissance portrait busts.

**"Donatello among the wild beasts"**
At the 1905 Salon d'Automne, critic Louis Vauxcelles saw a classical-style sculpture surrounded by brightly colored paintings by Matisse and his circle and quipped "Donatello chez les fauves" ("Donatello among the wild beasts"), giving Fauvism its name.
